items.title: A fitness function bans the wall clock
items.body:
The key is right. `AmbientTimeBanTests` walks every `.cs` file under `src/Atlas.Domain` and fails if a line matches `DateTime.Now`, `DateTime.UtcNow`, `DateTimeOffset.Now` or `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow`. Time must arrive as a parameter or from a `TimeProvider` at the edge.

- There is no analyzer that rewrites code; the test only reports offenders.
- `Directory.Build.props` sets `TreatWarningsAsErrors`, but no analyzer warns about `DateTime.Now`.
- A checklist depends on people remembering; the ledger calls a source-scanning fitness function stronger than any number of example tests.

excerpts.quote: DateTime\.Now|DateTime\.UtcNow|DateTimeOffset\.Now|DateTimeOffset\.UtcNow
A fitness function that *bans the pattern in source* is stronger than any number of example tests

items.title: Actual days, counting the hire day
items.body:
The key is right. `HireMonthFraction` takes `DateTime.DaysInMonth(hiredOn.Year, 3)` = 31 (March always has 31 days) and `daysWorked = 31 - 16 + 1` = 16, because the hire day itself counts. The fraction is 16/31.

- Atlas rejects the 30-day-month fiction and uses actual days.
- The `+ 1` includes the 16th, so it is 16 days, not 15.
- Accrual does post at the month start, but the hire month is the one prorated month.

excerpts.quote: int daysWorked = daysInMonth - hiredOn.Day + 1;
**Actual** days (16th of a 31-day month → 16/31)

items.title: Money-moving routes require the key
items.body:
The key is right. `IsMoneyMoving` returns true for a POST whose path ends in `/pay` or `/execute`. With no key on such a route the middleware throws `RequestValidationException`, which the exception handler maps to 400.

- The header is optional elsewhere, but mandatory on these routes.
- Authentication is separate; the middleware even lets anonymous requests through so auth can answer 401.
- Nothing is queued; the request is rejected at once.

excerpts.quote: path.EndsWith("/pay", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)

items.title: AddMonths clamps to the end of the month
items.body:
The key is right. `DateOnly.AddMonths` moves by calendar months and, when the target day does not exist, uses the last day of the target month. April has 30 days, so January 31 plus three months is April 30.

- .NET does not roll the extra day into May.
- Months are not converted into a fixed number of days; that is the myth the page defuses.
- No exception is thrown; clamping is the documented behaviour.

excerpts.quote: which clamps correctly (Jan 31 + 3 months → Apr 30, because Apr 31 does not exist).
**"Add a month" is not "add 30 days."**

items.title: Rounding twelve times loses four cents
items.body:
The key is right. 100,000 / 12 = 8,333.333..., rounded to 8,333.33. Twelve of those make 99,999.96. Largest-remainder allocation instead gives four months 8,333.34 and eight months 8,333.33, which add to exactly 100,000.00.

- 8,333.333 rounds down, not up, so the total is below 100,000.
- The errors all point the same way, so they add up rather than cancel.
- Each month loses a third of a cent, not a whole cent, so the loss is 4 cents, not 12.

excerpts.quote: applied twelve times — gives `99,999.96`.

items.title: A reused key with a new body is a client bug
items.body:
The key is right. The middleware hashes method, path and body. When a stored record exists for the key, it compares the hashes with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`; a mismatch throws `IdempotencyConflictException`. The exception handler maps that to 422 with its own `idempotency-conflict` problem type.

- Replaying would hide a real client bug; the page says to surface it.
- The stored response is never replaced by a second execution.
- 409 is not used here; it is a 422 by design.

excerpts.quote: was already used with a different request.
StatusCodes.Status422UnprocessableEntity, AtlasProblems.IdempotencyConflict,

items.title: Start here: Atlas is a payroll course read sprint by sprint
items.body:
Atlas is a multi-country payroll and HR backend in .NET, built as a course of fifteen sprints. You are meant to read it the way a senior engineer reviews code, starting from the domain and moving outwards.

This quest uses five short documents:

1. `docs/concepts/money-allocation.md`: splitting money without losing cents.
2. `docs/concepts/date-math.md`: why dates are business rules.
3. `docs/concepts/temporal-data.md`: three kinds of "history".
4. `docs/concepts/at-least-once.md`: events, retries and idempotency keys.
5. `docs/sprints/flaw-ledger.md`: five bugs planted on purpose and found later.

Each concept page names the code that implements it. Open that file next to the page and find the lines. The `LEARNER-GUIDE.md` explains the comment markers (`LEARN:`, `WHY:`, `GOTCHA:`) you will see in the code.

excerpts.quote: you are here to **read it the way a senior engineer would**, one sprint at a time.

readMore.why: How to study a sprint and how to read a hexagonal codebase.
The Money value object behind the allocation questions.

items.title: Examples convince; properties catch
items.body:
The key is right. A property test states an invariant over many inputs (here adversarial salaries in `[InlineData]` rows, standing in for a CsCheck property): for any salary, the twelve periods sum to the annual figure. The drift only shows on numbers that do not divide by twelve, which a single chosen example can easily miss.

- A golden file is one hand-checked worker; useful for auditors, weak at this class of bug.
- No architecture test bans division; architecture tests check dependencies.
- Comparing with last month says nothing about whether the year adds up.

excerpts.quote: They catch the class of bug a single example can't
the property test catches the rounding drift the auditor would never think to look for.

items.title: Core idea: rounding and date counting are business decisions
items.body:
Two kinds of code look like small utilities but really carry business rules. The first is splitting a money amount into parts: if each part is rounded on its own, the parts may not add back up to the whole. The second is date arithmetic: "how many days", "what is one month later", "what happens at the end of the year" each have several reasonable answers.

Atlas writes its answers down in the concept pages and pins each one with a test. While reading, list every choice the pages name and then find the method that makes it. Ask the three questions the date page suggests: whose clock, which day-count, what happens at the boundary.

excerpts.quote: it has left the land of utilities and entered the land of *policy*.
When you see date arithmetic in a diff, ask three questions

readMore.why: The leave-accrual fold with its documented policy choices.

items.title: Core idea: the network may deliver the same thing twice
items.body:
Atlas changes its database and also tells other systems about the change. Doing both at once is impossible without heavy machinery, so you have to pick which failure you can live with. The concept page compares the options and explains the transactional outbox.

The same page also covers the other direction: a client that times out may resend a payment request. Atlas uses an `Idempotency-Key` header so a resend does not pay twice. Read `at-least-once.md`, then open `IdempotencyMiddleware.cs` and follow what happens on the first request with a key and on a repeat.

excerpts.quote: there is no free lunch that updates both atomically.
You *can* make the receiver treat a duplicate as a no-op.

readMore.why: The middleware that replays responses for repeated keys.
Flaws 3 and 4 show these problems as real bugs.

items.title: Cap first, then earn the new year
items.body:
The key is right. In `AccruedThrough`, at each leave-year boundary except the hire year, `carried = Math.Min(carried, policy.CarryoverCapDays)` runs first, and only then is the new year's accrual added. So 12 becomes 5, and the full new entitlement is added on top.

- Accrue-then-cap is the other, stingier policy; the guide says both are tested and Atlas chose the first.
- The cap applies to the carried balance, not to new earnings.
- Only days above the cap are forfeited; 5 days carry over.

excerpts.quote: carried = Math.Min(carried, policy.CarryoverCapDays);
A fresh year always has room for its full entitlement.

items.title: The update endpoint performs an insert
items.body:
The key is right. `UpdateEmploymentTerms` builds a new employment record and calls `records.AddAsync(record, ...)`; the comment says APPEND and "Nothing is edited". History cannot be lost because there is no UPDATE to lose it, and a retroactive raise is just a record with a past `EffectiveFrom`.

- An audit entry is written too (`audit.Append(AuditEntry.Record(...))`, with before and after values), but no row is updated.
- No soft delete exists; the page calls it "not needed yet".
- No column is overwritten.

excerpts.quote: APPEND. Nothing is edited; history cannot be lost
The update endpoint for terms performs an INSERT.

items.title: A failed first try leaves nothing to replay
items.body:
The key is right. The middleware runs the request, then saves the captured response only `if (http.Response.StatusCode is >= 200 and < 300)`. A 503 is not stored, so the retry with the same key finds no prior record and executes normally.

- No 503 is replayed; the code comment says a 503 must stay retryable.
- 422 is for a key reused with a different body, which is not the case here.
- There is no lock or wait on keys in this middleware.

excerpts.quote: if (http.Response.StatusCode is >= 200 and < 300)
a transient 503 must stay retryable.

items.title: Publish-then-commit creates phantom events
items.body:
The key is right. With a sink that sends at once, the event is already out when `CommitAsync` fails and rolls back. Subscribers now believe in a change that does not exist: a phantom. The opposite order loses events on a crash. The outbox fixes both by writing the event as a row inside the same transaction.

- A rollback cannot recall a message already sent.
- Nothing retries the commit in that design.
- The planted sink did not buffer. Today's `IEventSink` is `OutboxEventSink`, which only stages a row in the transaction; that is the fix, not the flaw.

excerpts.quote: Transaction rolls back → you announced an event that never happened. A **phantom**.
a rolled-back transaction had already announced an event that never happened

items.title: How Allocate hands out the leftover cent
items.body:
The key is right. `Allocate` converts to minor units: 10.00 is 1000 cents. `each = 1000 / 3 = 333` and the remainder is 1. The loop gives one extra cent to the first `extra` shares (`i < extra`), so the result is 3.34, 3.33, 3.33, which sums to exactly 10.00.

- No cent is dropped or logged; the rule is that parts sum to the whole.
- `Allocate(3)` returns exactly three shares; no extra leftover share is added.
- Shares are built with `FromMinorUnits`, whole cents only.

excerpts.quote: long minor = each + (i < extra ? step : 0);
the shares must sum to **exactly** the original

items.title: Business dates have no time of day
items.body:
The key is right. Leave is counted in calendar days. A `DateTimeOffset` carries a time and an offset, so a leave day stored that way would have an invented time-of-day, and a timezone shift could move it to another date: the exact bug Atlas removed from probation math.

- Sorting speed is not the reason the page gives.
- `DateTimeOffset` covers dates far before 1970.
- EF Core can map `DateTimeOffset`; the choice is about meaning, not mapping.

excerpts.quote: would invent a fictional time-of-day and re-introduce the very timezone bug we just removed.
Effective dating runs on **business time** (`DateOnly`
